curriculum.subject: LANGUAGE_ARTS
curriculum.description: Introduce a specific topic using a clear introductory sentence paired with a simple definition. Focus: Defining a subject clearly at the start of an informative text. Examples: A mammal is an animal with fur, Sharks are fish that live in the ocean, The sun is a star that gives us light, An insect is a small bug with six legs, Seeds are what grow into plants, Clouds are made of water vapor, Planets move around the sun, Maps help us find places. Constraints: Use fill-in-the-blanks to complete topic introduction sentences.

status: authored; catalog-checked; each binding generator-probed once; not hydrated as a lesson; not runtime-tested
learnerAction: Write a first sentence that names the topic and says what kind of thing it is plus one feature ("A mammal is an animal with fur").

components.title: Meet a Topic Sentence
components.intent: Grade 2 informational paragraph about one animal or object. The model topic sentence must define the topic: name its category and one feature (A ___ is a ___ that ___). Child taps the topic sentence in the model, then writes their own with a frame.

components.title: Which Sentence Starts the Paragraph?
components.intent: Grade 2. Show a short informative paragraph with its first sentence missing. Options: one definition sentence (category + feature), one detail sentence from the body, one opinion, one off-topic sentence.

evidenceCriteria: Picks the defining sentence over a body detail (knowledge-check).
Writes "A/An [topic] is a [category] that/with [feature]" with a true category and feature. NOT currently judged by any primitive.
coverageLimits: paragraph-architect scores parts present, not quality: an empty frame counts as content (ParagraphArchitect.tsx:540-545, 693-697).
Its modes change only the prompt. Task and score are identical across informational, narrative and opinion.
The only scored right/wrong act is tapping the topic sentence in the model.

recommendation.rationale: Add a judged "define the topic" mode to paragraph-architect. The writing surface exists; what is missing is a check that the sentence names a category and a true feature. See brief 1.
